findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
findings.body: The new cleanup logging calls use Error unconditionally, including when fetching and deleting succeed and when no rows need cleanup. The same pattern appears in count-based cleanup and orphaned-tag cleanup. Normal background maintenance will therefore continually generate false error events, potentially triggering log-based alerts, and will emit every selected ID at the default logging level. Remove these diagnostic calls or move successful-batch logging to Debug without dumping entire ID lists.

findings.title: SQLite ID-list construction performs quadratic copying
findings.body: For SQLite batches larger than 999, each iteration formats a new string containing the entire accumulated ID list. Building a batch of N IDs therefore copies O(N²) bytes. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands, as explicitly supported by the new test, this creates gigabytes of temporary allocations per full batch and can substantially delay cleanup and increase GC pressure. Build the list with strings.Builder or an append-based byte buffer instead.

findings.title: The shorter ticker accelerates every cleanup job, not just annotations
findings.body: Changing this ticker from ten minutes to one minute makes all cleanup jobs run ten times as often, including filesystem scans, dashboard-version deletion, image deletion, and query-history limit enforcement. It also leaves the nine-minute execution timeout unchanged: if a cleanup cycle takes longer than one minute, a tick will already be pending when it finishes, allowing repeated cycles to run without a pause. This unrelated scheduling change can materially increase database and filesystem load. Preserve the existing interval for this annotation-query fix, or isolate and justify a separate scheduling change.
